sources.selection: scalerank <= 5 only. Natural Earth ships several thousand watercourses and this atlas wants the Loire, the Seine, the Rhone, the Garonne and the Danube — the rivers a reader recognises as the shape of a country. Hundreds of tiny streams would be the OpenStreetMap default look, which is the thing this cartography exists not to be.

sources.dataset: Natural Earth 1:50m lakes

sources.dataset: Natural Earth 1:50m marine polygons (sea and ocean names)

sources.dataset: Natural Earth 1:50m physical geography regions (ranges, plains)
sources.selection: Named ranges and basins — ALPS, PYRENEES, MASSIF CENTRAL — for the italic serif feature labels. This is the layer that lets a reader see where the Alps are before the DEM exists.

sources.dataset: Natural Earth 1:10m named elevation points (summits and depressions)
sources.selection: Named summits inside the extent, 105 of them, and only the highest few in any one frame. THE 1:50m FILE HAS THREE IN ALL OF EUROPE — Elbrus, Mont Blanc and one depression — which is not a layer. A peak with a measured height is the closest this atlas comes to relief without an elevation model, and it is a measurement somebody else made rather than a surface we fitted.

sources.dataset: AWS Terrain Tiles, terrarium encoding, zoom 6 tile 32/22
sources.selection: Zoom 6 and no deeper, and every tile that intersects the atlas extent. $comment_awaiting: AWAITING_FETCH: rows that are registered, licence-checked and NOT in the repository. The build must run on a host with no internet, so raw bytes are committed — and this environment's proxy refuses every general host, so acquisition is a human step. These are the layers the renderer declares and cannot draw. Each carries the same public-domain terms as the land already here, from the same publisher, so no new licence DECISION is waiting on anybody: only the command. `scripts/map/fetch.py --awaiting` fetches them; `checks.py` asserts each has a licence record and that its file is genuinely absent, so a half-fetched row cannot sit here looking settled.
